**On Glass**

Given the freedom to write about anything, I find myself drawn to a thing that is designed not to be noticed. Glass is the material we look through rather than at. It sits between us and nearly everything—the street outside, the words on a screen, the face in the bathroom mirror, the small print on a medicine bottle—and does its work by disappearing. Most days no one thinks about it at all. That seems like a good reason to spend some time thinking about it now.

Start with where it comes from, which is almost nothing. Glass is sand that has been persuaded to forget it was sand. Heat silica hot enough, add something to lower the melting point—soda, potash, the ashes of certain plants—and something to stabilize the result, usually lime, and you get a liquid that, when cooled quickly enough, never quite manages to reorganize itself into crystals. It freezes in disorder. Its atoms are caught mid-gesture, arranged the way they would be in a liquid but locked in place. This is why glass is transparent: there are no grain boundaries or crystal faces to scatter light, just a smooth continuous jumble that light can pass through as if through water that has stopped moving.

Nature makes glass on its own, occasionally and dramatically. Lightning striking a beach can fuse a tube of sand into a fulgurite, a knobbly hollow branch of glass shaped like the bolt that made it. Volcanoes produce obsidian, and for hundreds of thousands of years obsidian was the sharpest thing a human hand could hold; a freshly knapped obsidian edge is thinner than a steel scalpel's. And there is the strange pale-yellow glass scattered across a patch of the Libyan desert, formed some twenty-nine million years ago when something from space struck or exploded above the sand. A piece of it was carved into a scarab and set in a pectoral buried with Tutankhamun. Someone found that glass in the desert, three thousand years ago, and recognized that it was extraordinary without having any idea what it was.

The made kind begins in Mesopotamia and Egypt around 3500 BCE, and it begins small. The first glass objects are beads. For roughly two thousand years, glass was essentially a jewelry material, a way to imitate lapis lazuli and turquoise and carnelian, precious stones that had to be traded across enormous distances. Glass could be colored to match them and was, to a Bronze Age eye, a kind of alchemical triumph: stone made from fire. It was rare, expensive, and controlled by palace workshops. The earliest vessels were formed by winding molten glass around a core of clay and dung, then scraping the core out after cooling. They are small, thick-walled, beautiful, and opaque. Transparency was not the point. Color was the point.

Pliny the Elder, writing in the first century CE, tells a story about the discovery of glass that he himself seems to half-believe. Some Phoenician merchants carrying natron—a natural soda—landed on a beach at the mouth of a river in what is now Israel, and, lacking stones to prop their cooking pots over the fire, used blocks of natron instead. The heat fused the natron with the beach sand, and translucent streams of a new liquid ran out. The story is almost certainly false as history, and almost certainly true as chemistry. It is the recipe for glass disguised as an anecdote, and it has the shape of all good origin stories: something valuable comes from an accident, on a shore, at a meal.

The real revolution came later, and its exact author is unknown. Sometime in the first century BCE, on the Syro-Palestinian coast, someone figured out that you could gather a blob of molten glass on the end of a hollow tube and blow into it. This sounds like a small thing. It changed everything about what glass was for. Core-forming was slow and produced one small vessel at a time; blowing was fast, and it produced thin-walled vessels of almost any size and shape. Glass went from being a luxury to being cheap. Within a century or two, Roman households across the empire were full of it—cups, bottles, jars, storage vessels, perfume flasks, the square-shouldered bottles that packed efficiently into crates. Archaeologists find Roman glass everywhere, in quantities that would have been unimaginable a few generations before blowing. It is the first mass-produced glass, and its ubiquity in the ground is a kind of testimony: this is how a material becomes ordinary.

The Romans also put glass in windows, which is a stranger idea than it sounds. A window is a hole in a wall that you want to keep as a hole—for light—while not having it be a hole—for wind, rain, cold, thieves. Before glass, the solutions were shutters, oiled cloth, thin-scraped animal skin, sheets of translucent stone like alabaster or mica. All of them let in some light and blocked the view. Roman window glass, cast in slabs, was thick and greenish and not very clear, but it was the beginning of a peculiar relationship between people and the outside that would take another fifteen centuries to fully develop: the ability to see out while staying in.

After Rome, the great glass of the West was not clear at all. It was the stained glass of the cathedrals, and it inverted the relationship with light. A window at Chartres is not for looking through. It is for being looked at, or rather for being looked *into*, and what it does with the light coming from behind is transform it—turn plain daylight into a wall of saturated color that seems to originate inside the glass itself. Medieval glassmakers were artists of impurity. They colored glass with metal oxides, cobalt for blue, copper for green and red, manganese for purple, and the glass was valued precisely for what it added to the light rather than for what it let pass unchanged. Clarity was not yet a virtue.

That changed in Venice. Or more precisely on Murano, the island where the city's glassmakers were sent in 1291, officially because their furnaces were a fire hazard and unofficially because it made them easier to watch. Murano's glassmakers were among the most privileged craftsmen in Europe—they could marry into noble families—and also among the most confined; leaving the Republic with trade secrets was treated as something close to treason. Around the middle of the fifteenth century, a glassmaker named Angelo Barovier is credited with perfecting *cristallo*: glass so clear and colorless it was named for rock crystal, the natural quartz it imitated. The trick involved purifying the plant-ash alkali and adding manganese as a decolorizer to cancel out the greenish tint from iron impurities. The result was a material that, for the first time in history, could be made deliberately and reliably to look like almost nothing.

Consider how odd it is to prize a material for its absence. Every other craft material—wood, stone, metal, cloth, clay—is admired for its presence, its grain, its heft, its color, its surface. Cristallo was admired because you could forget it was there. It is a material whose highest achievement is self-erasure, and its arrival marks a shift in what people wanted from the world. They wanted to see it plainly.

And then, once glass could be made clear, the seeing began in earnest.

Spectacles appear in northern Italy in the late thirteenth century, before cristallo, using convex lenses of reasonably clear glass or crystal to correct farsightedness. They were probably invented by a craftsman rather than a scholar, and for a long time nobody knew who. Their effect on intellectual life is hard to overstate. Before spectacles, a scribe or scholar's working life was essentially over when presbyopia set in around forty-five; after them, the productive life of a reader could extend another twenty or thirty years. It is one of those technologies that does not announce itself as transformative—it is a small thing worn on the nose—but that quietly doubles the useful lifespan of an entire class of skilled people.

Then, in a burst around 1600, glass gave humans two new sets of eyes. The telescope, assembled in the Netherlands in 1608 and improved and pointed skyward by Galileo the following year, revealed that the moon had mountains, that Jupiter had moons of its own, that the Milky Way was made of stars, and that Venus showed phases like the moon—an observation that was very difficult to reconcile with the Earth sitting at the center of everything. A few decades later the microscope, another Dutch invention, showed Robert Hooke the cells in a slice of cork and showed Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a draper who ground his own tiny lenses, that a drop of pond water was crowded with living things nobody had ever suspected. The universe got very much larger and very much smaller in the same century, and the instrument in both cases was a curved piece of clear glass.

It is worth pausing on the fact that this could only happen once glass was transparent enough and could be ground precisely enough. The telescope is an idea that almost anyone might have had—two lenses in a tube—but it is an idea that requires a material. The historians Alan Macfarlane and Gerry Martin made a provocative argument about this some years ago: that the development of clear glass in Western Europe, and its relative neglect in China and Japan, helps explain why experimental science took the shape it did where it did. The East Asian civilizations knew glass and were not much interested in it; they had porcelain for vessels, paper for windows, polished bronze for mirrors, and did not develop the tradition of lens-grinding that made the seventeenth-century instruments possible. The argument is contested, and should be—it is too neat to attribute the scientific revolution to a single material—but there is something to the observation that a culture's tools shape what it can discover, and that the tool of transparency is unusually consequential.

Glass also gave people a new way to see themselves. Mirrors before the Renaissance were polished metal, dim and slightly warped. Venetian glassmakers learned to back a sheet of flat glass with an amalgam of tin and mercury, producing mirrors of a clarity that startled people. A Venetian mirror in the sixteenth century could cost more than a painting by a master. It is not a coincidence that the self-portrait flourishes in exactly the period when good mirrors become available; Dürer, Rembrandt, and their contemporaries were looking into a material that had not existed a few generations before. The mirror is glass turned back on the viewer, transparency reversed into reflection, and it introduced a new intimacy with one's own face—and perhaps a new self-consciousness—that we now take entirely for granted.

The nineteenth century made glass big. The Crystal Palace, built in Hyde Park in 1851 to house the Great Exhibition, was a building made almost entirely of iron and glass—nearly three hundred thousand panes—and it looked, to people who had never seen such a thing, like a building made of air. Joseph Paxton, its designer, was a gardener; he had learned how to build glass houses to grow water lilies for a duke, and he simply scaled up. The greenhouse became architecture. The twentieth century took the idea further, and the glass curtain wall became the default skin of the modern city, buildings that reflect each other and the sky and seem to have no inside at all. There is a small irony here: the material that made it possible to see out also made it possible to be seen, and the glass office tower is both a window and a display case.

Somewhere along the way a myth attached itself to glass that is worth dispelling because it is so appealing. People say that glass is really a liquid, just an extremely slow one, and that the windows in old cathedrals are thicker at the bottom because the glass has been flowing downward for centuries. It is a lovely image and it is wrong. Glass is an amorphous solid; the time it would take a window pane to flow perceptibly at room temperature is longer than the age of the universe by a comfortable margin. Old windows are uneven because they were made unevenly—medieval crown glass was spun into a disc and cut into panes of varying thickness—and glaziers, sensibly, tended to set the heavy edge down. The myth persists, I think, because glass really is caught between states. It is a liquid that forgot to become a crystal, a solid that never got organized. It is in-between, and we sense that about it even when we misdescribe it.

The most recent transformation is the strangest. In 1966 a young engineer named Charles Kao proposed that if you could make glass pure enough—far purer than any window—you could send light down a hair-thin fiber for kilometers with very little loss. Four years later researchers at Corning made a fiber that did it. Today the oceans are crossed by cables full of glass strands, each carrying pulses of light that encode everything: this sentence, if you are reading it somewhere far from where it was written, has almost certainly traveled through glass to reach you. Glass, which began as a way to imitate gemstones, has become the medium of language itself. The screen you may be reading on is glass too, a sheet chemically strengthened so it can be tapped and dropped and carried in a pocket, a thin transparent membrane between a person and a world of light behind it.

So the arc runs like this: beads, then bottles, then windows, then colored light in churches, then clarity, then lenses that revealed the very large and the very small, then mirrors that revealed the self, then buildings made of sky, then strands carrying voices under the sea. Through every stage the material was made of the same thing—melted sand, the most common stuff on any shore—and through every stage after Murano its excellence was measured by how completely it could vanish.

I said glass is the material we look through rather than at, and I think that is why it interests me. There is a whole category of things whose success is measured by invisibility. Good translation, good typography, good infrastructure, good manners, the pane in the window—they all work best when no one notices them working, and they are noticed mainly when they fail: the cracked screen, the awkward sentence, the pipe that bursts. Glass is the physical emblem of that category, the clearest case of a made thing whose entire purpose is to get out of the way of something else. It sits between us and nearly everything, and it asks only not to be seen.

But it is there. It has a history, a chemistry, a set of choices behind it. Someone decided that clarity was worth pursuing. Someone ground a lens and pointed it at Jupiter. Someone purified silica until light could travel through it for a hundred kilometers. All of that is present in the window, holding the weather out and letting the light in, waiting patiently to be overlooked. It seems only fair, once in a while, to look at it instead.
